stem: A pregnant client is being evaluated for preeclampsia. The nurse notes an elevated serum uric acid level, but the client's blood pressure and the other findings needed for ACOG diagnostic criteria have not yet been established. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.A: The uric acid result alone confirms preeclampsia and no further diagnostic assessment is needed.
options.B: The uric acid result alone establishes preeclampsia with severe features even without a qualifying severe-feature finding.
options.C: The uric acid result should not be used by itself to diagnose or classify preeclampsia; the nurse should evaluate the established blood-pressure and organ-dysfunction/proteinuria criteria.
options.D: The uric acid result rules out preeclampsia if it later returns to the laboratory reference range.

rationale: C is correct. Current ACOG diagnostic criteria for preeclampsia are based on new-onset hypertension together with proteinuria or qualifying new end-organ findings; severe-feature classification uses defined findings such as severe-range blood pressure, thrombocytopenia, renal insufficiency, impaired liver function, pulmonary edema, persistent neurologic symptoms, or visual disturbance. Serum uric acid is not one of the ACOG criteria listed for establishing or classifying preeclampsia. Therefore, an elevated uric acid result should not independently confirm preeclampsia or a severe-feature classification, and a normal value cannot independently rule the disorder out. The nurse should interpret the result only within the full clinical assessment rather than treating it as a stand-alone diagnostic test.
educational_objective: Use established blood-pressure, proteinuria, and end-organ criteria to diagnose and classify preeclampsia rather than using an isolated serum uric acid result as a stand-alone diagnostic or exclusionary test.
source_organization: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG)
source_document_title: Countdown to Intern Year, Week 3: Hypertensive Disorders; Preeclampsia and High Blood Pressure During Pregnancy
source_version_date: Current ACOG web guidance accessed 2026-08-17; criteria reflect Practice Bulletin No. 222 framework
source_locator: Countdown to Intern Year, Week 3 — 'Criteria for Preeclampsia +/- Severe Features': preeclampsia is elevated blood pressure plus proteinuria or new-onset end-organ damage; listed end-organ criteria include thrombocytopenia, renal insufficiency, impaired liver function, pulmonary edema, and specified neurologic/visual symptoms. 'Preeclampsia with Severe Features' lists the defined severe-feature criteria. Preeclampsia and High Blood Pressure During Pregnancy FAQ — diagnosis section: high blood pressure is confirmed and urine, liver, kidney, and platelet testing may be used; severe features are separately enumerated. Serum uric acid is not included among these diagnostic or severe-feature criteria.
source_claim_supported: ACOG's diagnostic and severe-feature criteria for preeclampsia do not use serum uric acid as a stand-alone diagnostic, severity-classification, or exclusion criterion; diagnosis must be based on the established blood-pressure and qualifying proteinuria/end-organ findings.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: monitor laboratory values and recognize trends or changes that can indicate potential complications; distinguish clinically meaningful diagnostic findings from nondefinitive laboratory data.
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — correct interpretation of laboratory data during preeclampsia evaluation
correction_summary: The source item's claim that elevated uric acid 'supports' preeclampsia lacked a sufficiently exact current ACOG locator. Rather than preserve that weakly sourced assertion, the item was rebuilt around the directly verifiable ACOG diagnostic framework: uric acid is not a listed stand-alone diagnostic or severe-feature criterion, and established blood-pressure plus proteinuria/end-organ criteria must drive classification.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.clinical_category: preeclampsia evaluation / laboratory interpretation / diagnostic criteria
audit_findings.source_audit: The original generic ACOG citation did not directly support the asserted role of uric acid. Current ACOG public criteria were verified instead and provide an exact exhaustive diagnostic/severe-feature framework that does not include uric acid as a stand-alone criterion.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: C limits the claim to what is directly supported: diagnostic classification should use the listed ACOG criteria. A and B incorrectly promote one unlisted laboratory value to a definitive diagnostic or severity test. D incorrectly makes a normal uric acid result exclusionary.
audit_findings.choice_A: Incorrect; an isolated uric acid elevation is not one of ACOG's stand-alone diagnostic criteria.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; severe-feature classification requires one of the defined severe findings, not uric acid alone.
audit_findings.choice_C: Correct; it directs interpretation back to the established ACOG criteria without overclaiming what uric acid means.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; a normal uric acid result is not an ACOG rule-out criterion.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: The final item no longer depends on whether uric acid is epidemiologically associated with preeclampsia. It tests only whether the isolated value is sufficient for ACOG diagnosis/classification, for which C is the sole defensible answer.
audit_findings.cueing: All four options address diagnostic use of the same laboratory result and are comparable in scope; none relies on an obviously unrelated mechanism.
audit_findings.blueprint: The item tests appropriate interpretation of laboratory information and avoidance of overreliance on a nondefinitive result, fitting Reduction of Risk Potential.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechallenged the item for the possibility that uric acid may correlate with disease severity in some literature. The final question deliberately makes no claim about correlation; it asks only whether the isolated value is an ACOG diagnostic or severe-feature criterion. Verified the current ACOG criteria list again and found no competing answer. No unresolved conflict remained.
